Rocks make up the lithosphere. Hydrocarbons sit in the pore spaces of rocks. Porosity = total void volume ÷ total rock volume (quoted as a percentage). It exists mainly in rocks made of grains rather than interlocking crystals. The three rock types:

IgneousMetamorphicSedimentary
Formed byCrystallisation of molten materialRecrystallisation of older rock by heat (thermal) or heat + pressure and deformation (regional)Accumulation of particles, then burial, compaction and cementation
Share of crust~96%–Large majority of petroleum reservoirs and source rocks
Porosity / permeabilityVery low or none (except gas bubbles in lavas)None (often fractured)Can be high
Drilling target?Rarely (fractured granite and lava occasionally; can be seals)RarelyYes: the main targets
ExamplesBasalt, granite, gabbroSlate, schist, gneiss, marble, quartziteSandstone, mudstone, limestone

Igneous rocks

  • Extrusive (lavas and tuffs, from volcanoes): cool fast, so fine crystals (often too fine to see). Often contain gas bubbles. Basalt, andesite, rhyolite.
  • Intrusive (pushed into existing rock): cool slowly because there is less temperature difference with the surroundings, so coarse, easily visible crystals. Granite, gabbro, diorite. Melts that intrude at high crustal levels cool faster and give medium to fine crystals.
  • Intrusions that cut across the strata are dikes. Intrusions that go along the layers are sills.

Metamorphic rocks

Thermal metamorphism happens around hot igneous intrusions. Regional metamorphism goes with deep burial and mountain building. The bulk composition does not change: limestone becomes marble, quartz sandstone becomes quartzite, and muddy rocks become schists and gneisses. At extreme burial they melt and are recycled as igneous rocks (the rock cycle).

Sedimentary rocks and basins

Sediments need space to accumulate and be buried. That space is a basin, a regional area of active subsidence, always linked to deformation of the crust (often plate tectonics). Sedimentary rocks are classified by what they are made of:

TypeFormed byExamplesReservoir quality
Clastic (detrital)Erosion of older rock, transport by water or air, deposition, burial, compaction, cementationConglomerates, sandstones, mudstonesCoarser grain sizes often very porous and permeable; fine grains tend to be impermeable
ChemicalDirect precipitation of minerals from waterLimestones, evaporitesCrystalline, so impermeable
OrganicAccumulated remains of animals or plantsLimestones, chert, coalLimestones can be very porous and permeable; the others are relatively impermeable

Clastic rocks (quartz, feldspar and other silica-based minerals and rock fragments) are also called siliciclastic. Another common industry grouping is carbonate rocks (CaCO3 or Ca(Mg)CO3: limestone, dolostone), which are chemical or organic in origin.

What controls porosity and permeability

  • Texture: grain size, sorting, shape, roundness and packing. The highest porosity is generally in well-sorted, medium to coarse sandstones. Conglomerates are poorly sorted, which reduces void space. Mudstones compact so well during burial that pore space is greatly reduced.
  • Permeability depends on pore size and on the size of the pore connections (throats). Larger pores with good connections give higher permeability. Sandstones tend to have the largest connected pore space.
  • Cementation and compaction during burial fill and shrink pores, so deeply buried and older rocks usually have lower porosity and permeability than shallow, young ones.
  • Sedimentary structures (bedding, laminae) come from the depositional process (gravity flows, various strengths of fluid flow, settling from suspension), which depends on the depositional environment (e.g. rivers = fluvial, beaches = shallow marine). Layering makes porosity and permeability heterogeneous, which affects the production strategy.

Stratigraphy

Stratigraphy is the study of layers (strata), i.e. the history of deposition, the geological record. Types, by what is analysed:

  • Lithostratigraphy: rock types.
  • Biostratigraphy: fossil content (very useful for age and depositional environment).
  • Chemostratigraphy: chemical composition. Magnetostratigraphy: magnetic signatures.
  • Sequence stratigraphy: grouping of layers into sequences.
  • Chronostratigraphy / geochronology: subdivision of rocks by time, and time itself.

Guiding principles

  • "The present is key to the past": processes acting today acted in the past, so we can infer past environments and what their rocks look like.
  • Steno's three principles (17th century): original horizontality (sediment is laid down on a flat surface by gravity), superposition (in undisturbed strata, younger on older), original continuity (layers extend sideways until they meet an obstacle, taper out or grade into another sediment). Modern stratigraphers accept that layers can be deposited slightly inclined and that lateral lithology changes are important.
  • Walther's Law (1894): lithostratigraphic transitions in a conformable vertical sequence reflect laterally migrating environments. Adjacent layers should come from adjacent environments. If two lithologies in a vertical sequence could not have been deposited in adjacent environments, an unconformity (erosion or non-deposition) lies between them.
  • Processes act on what is already there: any folding, faulting or intrusion must be younger than the layers it affects. This gives the relative order of events.

Gaps in the record

The preserved record is only a small part of elapsed time. Small gaps are hiatuses, big gaps (millions of years) are unconformities:

  • Angular unconformity: older strata were tilted or deformed (tectonics), then eroded, then new layers deposited on top.
  • Disconformity: parallel strata with evidence of erosion between them.
  • Paraconformity: parallel strata, gap caused by a period of non-deposition.

Geological time scale

Ages are in Ma (million years before present) and refer to the boundary with the older unit below. The Precambrian (before ~542 Ma) is generally of no interest to petroleum geologists: reservoir quality is low and there is no concentrated organic matter for source rocks. After the explosion of life at the base of the Cambrian, organic-rich source rocks became possible and petroleum systems developed.

EraPeriod (age of base, Ma)
CenozoicQuaternary (Pleistocene 2) · Tertiary: Pliocene 5, Miocene 23, Oligocene 34, Eocene 56, Paleocene 65
MesozoicCretaceous 146 · Jurassic 200 · Triassic 251
PaleozoicPermian 299 · Carboniferous 359 · Devonian 416 · Silurian 444 · Ordovician 488 · Cambrian 542
PrecambrianEverything before 542 Ma

Geological structures

Strata are deformed over time by stress and strain during burial or plate movements. Deformation is plastic (rock bends without breaking: folding) or brittle (rock breaks: faulting and fracturing). Folds and faults are always younger than the layers they affect. Structural changes create the shapes in a reservoir layer that act as traps.

Describing orientation

  • Planar features (beds, faults): strike and dip. Strike is a horizontal line on the inclined surface, recorded as a compass bearing. Dip is at right angles to strike, the angle between the plane and the horizontal (measured with a clinometer).
  • Linear features (fold axes, lineations, slickensides): trend (compass bearing) and plunge (angle from horizontal).

Faults and fractures

  • Fault: a break with significant movement across the plane. Fracture: a break without significant movement.
  • Strike-slip (horizontal movement): sinistral (left-lateral) or dextral (right-lateral), judged by standing on one side and looking across the fault.
  • Dip-slip (vertical movement): normal or reverse, depending on whether the hanging wall (the block overlying the dipping fault plane) moves down or up. Oblique-slip combines both.
  • A real fault is often a thick fault zone with sets of related faults. That complexity makes faults either much more or much less permeable than the surrounding rock, so they can be conduits for migration or barriers to flow within a reservoir.
  • Faults create traps by offsetting reservoir layers against sealing layers, or by being sealing themselves.

Folds

  • Rock bent but not broken. Anticline = upfold. Syncline = downfold. A monoclinal fold has a steep or vertical limb.
  • The fold axis is the line of maximum curvature between the limbs. If it is not horizontal the fold is plunging.
  • Anticlines are ideal traps: they naturally form an enclosed high spot where hydrocarbons accumulate against a seal. Multiple or changing plunge directions are even better, and a dome is an anticline without a linear axis.

The petroleum play

What you need

  1. A source of carbon and hydrogen (organic matter).
  2. A suitable environment to turn it into petroleum (burial, heat, time).
  3. Porous and permeable rock to hold and move petroleum.
  4. A local geological trap for a commercial accumulation.

The play concept integrates all the information to decide where accumulations are likely. Its parts: source rock (and maturity) · migration (primary, secondary, timing) · reservoir rock · seal rock · trap.

Source rock and maturity

  • Organic matter buried with rock under high pressure and moderate to high temperature (below about 200 °C) converts to kerogen, then to mobile hydrocarbon. At least about 1 km of burial is needed, depending on the geothermal gradient.
  • Only a small share of the rock is organic and only a small share of that converts, so a large volume of source rock is needed. A good source rock has more than 5% organic matter: marine or marginal marine (lagoonal) mudrocks (especially from anoxic waters), lacustrine (lake) mudrocks, and coals.
  • Organic matter is only preserved if it is not exposed to oxygen (which oxidises it) and to organisms that would eat it, so source rocks tend to form in anoxic environments.
  • Immature: burial insufficient to convert organic matter. Mature: the right temperature has been reached and hydrocarbons are or have been generated. Over-mature: buried beyond the generation window, organic matter converted to graphite.

Migration

  • Primary migration (expulsion): generating hydrocarbons expands in volume, fracturing the source rock and letting the hydrocarbons escape into the surrounding rock.
  • Secondary migration: hydrocarbons are lighter than water, so buoyancy drives them upward through the pore spaces of the surrounding rocks (also affected by hydrodynamic flow).
  • They keep rising until they reach the surface, unless a seal (impermeable layer) stops them. Even then they travel along beneath the seal until they find a way up, unless a trap exists: reservoir and seal arranged in a shape that lets hydrocarbons in but stops further upward or sideways movement.
Timing is critical. The reservoir, seal and trap must all form before the hydrocarbons are generated and migrate. If they form later, the hydrocarbons may already have been lost.

Fluids in the trap

  • Oil and gas displace the original pore water, but some water always remains (often chemically attracted to mineral surfaces), so hydrocarbon saturation rarely reaches 100%: usually about 60 to 90%.
  • Fluids separate by density: gas on top, oil beneath, water (brine) at the bottom.

Types of trap

TypeFormedExamples
StratigraphicDuring deposition of the reservoir bedsUnconformity, lenticular (beds pinching out)
StructuralBy tectonic processes after depositionAnticline/dome, fault, salt dome plug
CombinationBoth (most likely in practice)e.g. a folded, pinching-out sand

From data to discovery

Outcrops at basin margins give rock types, stratigraphy and depositional environments. Seismic reflection gives the large-scale architecture of strata (next chapter). Geologists build correlations and maps and then risk maps showing where exploration is more or less likely to succeed. Specific areas to investigate are leads (which may need more detailed seismic). Something worth drilling is a prospect. A well that finds hydrocarbons is a discovery. Any well only samples one location, so size and shape are inferred from several wells. After a discovery the field is appraised (boundaries, fluid contacts, size and shape, reservoir properties, structural complexity), an economic analysis is made, and the company decides whether to develop.

Uncertainty

All maps and correlations are interpretations by a geologist or team, based on the quantity and quality of the available data. They will probably change as data arrives, so every conclusion has uncertainty and all exploration has risk. Managing and quantifying that risk is a core part of assessment, exploration and reservoir management.
notes.3:
No geophysical method measures oil directly. Geophysics applies physics to the study of subsurface geology: sediment thickness and the shape of structures that might trap oil. It usually follows the geological survey and comes before drilling. Where there are no surface clues (swamp, desert, offshore) it is the only practical way to explore.

Learning outcomes. Be able to: name the geophysical methods and what each measures · say which rocks magnetic and gravity surveys detect · explain why seismic is more important than magnetic and gravity · state the output and working principle of a seismic survey and the key wave properties · compare 2D, 3D and 4D surveys · compare land and marine surveys and their sources · calculate wave velocity (f, λ), acoustic impedance, reflection coefficient and two-way time.

Geophysical methods

MethodMeasuresUse
MagneticAnomalies in Earth's magnetic field caused by magnetic properties of rocksReconnaissance
GravityAnomalies in Earth's gravitational field caused by rock densityReconnaissance
SeismicTime taken for sound waves to travel through rocksReconnaissance and almost always detailed surveys
  • Reconnaissance surveys outline possible areas of interest: thick sediments and the possibility of structural traps.
  • Detailed surveys define well locations to test specific structures.

Magnetic surveys

  • The igneous and metamorphic basement is magnetic to varying degrees and creates anomalies. Sedimentary rocks are practically non-magnetic. So a measurement above a sedimentary basin is separated from the source of the anomaly by the thickness of the sediments.
  • Anomaly size relates to distance from its source, so the method gives the thickness of sediment over the basement and can reveal the basement's major tectonic trends.
  • Lava flows and igneous intrusions in the sediments have strong magnetic effects and can be detected.
  • The Earth's field is weak: about 60,000 gammas vertical at the magnetic poles and about half that horizontal at the magnetic equator (a small horseshoe magnet gives roughly 1000 times more). Anomalies of interest are a few to a few hundred gammas, and magnetometers read to a few hundredths of a gamma.
  • The field is recorded continuously (with a ground magnetometer, to check for magnetic storms). Results are corrected for variations in the field, survey errors and known regional effects, then contoured on a map.

Gravity surveys

  • Basement rocks are generally denser than overlying sediments, so gravity is high where basement comes near the surface and low over basement depressions. This outlines basin development and structural trends.
  • Older, denser rocks brought up in the cores of anticlines also give high gravity values.
  • Salt is less dense than surrounding rock, so salt domes show as low gravity anomalies.
  • Gravity varies from 983.221 gal at the poles to 978.048 gal at the equator. Significant anomalies are about 0.001 gal, so the working unit is the milligal. Gravimeters resolve about 0.01 mGal (one part in a million of Earth's field).
  • Instrument height must be known for each reading and rough terrain makes it slow. On ships the instrument sits on a gyroscopically stabilised platform.
  • Traverses are 0.5 to 1 mile apart. Readings are corrected for elevation, latitude, topography and diurnal variations, then contoured.
  • Interpreting anomalies needs the shapes of the subsurface structures, which are not known during exploration. So gravity data mostly provides leads for further geophysical exploration.

Seismic surveys

Seismic gives more detail on the shape and depth of structures than any other method, so it is the most used. A man-made source sends sound into the ground. Geophones measure the travel time and convert the motion to electric current, which goes to a seismograph (amplifier and recorder) to produce a seismogram. Travel time depends on rock density, depth and mineralogy. Records rarely exceed about 6 s and are measured to 0.001 s. Local velocity variation within a formation makes interpretation complicated.

Main outputs: (i) an image of subsurface structure and stratigraphy, (ii) rock and fluid properties, (iii) a static reservoir geo-model, (iv) monitoring and updating of the dynamic reservoir simulation model.

Working principles of seismic

Waves and velocity

The sound pulse contains a range of frequencies. As a wave passes between media, frequency is conserved but wavelength changes as velocity changes:

f = V / λ

The velocity of a P-wave depends on the rock's elastic properties and density:

V = sqrt( (K + 4G/3) / ρ ) K = bulk modulus = dP / (dv/v) G = shear modulus = shear stress / shear strain

(ρ = density, v = volume, P = pressure.) This equation is for the P (primary / pressure) wave, the fastest, which is what seismic interpretation mostly uses. S (shear) waves are mostly for research.

Reflection

At an interface part of the energy is reflected and part transmitted, so less energy reaches deeper targets. Energy is also lost with distance and with the properties of the medium (dispersion and attenuation). The main thing used to identify an interface is the reflected energy pattern, described by the reflection coefficient:

I = V × ρ (acoustic impedance) R12 = (I2 - I1) / (I1 + I2)
  • Layer 1 is above, layer 2 below. Sign of R = polarity. If I2 > I1 then R > 0 (positive polarity). The change in polarity helps identify the interface.
  • Velocity can go up or down across a boundary, but the variation of impedance is monotonic with the contrast. A big impedance contrast means a strong reflection; a near-zero contrast gives almost no reflection.

Depth from two-way time

TWT = 2d / V so d = TWT × V / 2

TWT (two-way time) is the down-and-back travel time, so depth uses half of it. It is recorded to the nearest millisecond: for V = 4000 m/s a 1 ms precision equals 0.001/2 × 4000 = 2 m.

Acquisition: geophones and spreads

  • Reflected energy is recorded by groups of geophones at equal spacing (50 or 100 m) along a line, with 24, 48 or up to 96 groups per shot. With 50 m spacing the spread length is therefore 1200 m to 4800 m.
  • Geophones record all ground movement, so the record includes noise from natural and man-made sources and from the shot itself. Noise is reduced by varying the number and spacing of geophones in a group, using a pattern of shot holes instead of one shot, and electrical filters.
  • The biggest improvement in signal to noise comes from common depth point (CDP) shooting: the source and geophones are moved along the line between shots, giving multiple records of reflections from the same subsurface points. The number of stations moved between shots sets the multiplicity of cover. The records for each CDP are added in processing: reflections add up, random noise cancels.

2D, 3D and 4D surveys

SurveyAcquisitionGives / used for
2DAlong a single lineA cross-section of the reservoir
3DAlong many parallel lines, forming a cubeA volume image. Needs a large oil volume expected to justify the cost.
4DRepeated 3D surveys at time intervalsMonitoring changes in fluid levels and pressure, so the dynamic reservoir model can be updated. Much attention in recent years.

Land and marine surveys

LandMarine
SourceSmall explosive charge in a shallow drilled hole; or a vibrating plate (Vibroseis truck). Formerly a falling weight.No dynamite: compressed air or gas exploding underwater, or an underwater electric discharge, towed behind the ship at a suitable depth
ReceiversGeophones laid on the groundGeophones in a neutrally buoyant cable towed by the same ship that holds the recording equipment
SpeedSlower (shot holes must be drilled)Faster in good weather: no holes, the spread moves continuously
MultiplicityLowerGenerally higher

Vibrating sources have much less energy than dynamite, but adding the signals from repeated vibrations improves the signal-to-noise ratio to compensate.

Interpreting seismic results

The object is to locate and detail structural traps. The initial programme of lines depends on existing knowledge: widely spaced reconnaissance lines over unexplored ground, or a detailed survey to help place development wells.

  • After processing, travel times are plotted on maps and contours drawn through equal time values. These are time-contour (isochron) maps, one per formation, showing all structural features.
  • For exploration, depth-contour maps are more convenient. Picking reflection horizons and contouring are done by computer, which also converts time to depth.
  • Time to depth needs the right velocity for each area. Typical values: about 4000 ft/s for unconsolidated near-surface sediment, 6000 to 13000 ft/s for sandstones and shales, 14000 to 20000 ft/s for limestone. Significant velocity variation in an area can change the shape of contours noticeably after conversion.
  • Measuring velocity: directly, by lowering a geophone into a well and timing shots from the surface to various depths. Before the first well is drilled, velocity comes from a statistical analysis of the seismic data. After drilling, a continuous velocity log confirms it, with its integration checked against direct geophone travel times at selected depths.

Worked examples

1. Reflection coefficients

Rock properties: granite V = 5.0 km/s, ρ = 2700 kg/m³; limestone 6.0, 2300; sandstone 4.2, 2500; shale 2.5, 2300. First get impedance I = V × ρ (use V in km/s as the tutorial does; only the ratio matters):

RockV, km/sρ, kg/m³I = V×ρ
Granite5.0270013,500
Limestone6.0230013,800
Sandstone4.2250010,500
Shale2.523005,750
a) top limestone, bottom shale: R = (5750 - 13800) / (5750 + 13800) = -0.4 b) top shale, bottom sandstone: R = (10500 - 5750) / (10500 + 5750) = +0.3 c) top limestone, bottom granite: R = (13500 - 13800) / (13500 + 13800) = -0.01

Reading the answers: R is negative where the wave moves into a lower-impedance layer (a) and positive where it moves into a higher-impedance layer (b). In (c) the impedances are almost equal, so there is almost no reflection and the interface is nearly invisible. Always put the layer the wave reaches second (the lower layer) as I2.

2. Depth from TWT

TWT = 0.001 s, V = 6 km/s = 6000 m/s:

d = TWT × V / 2 = 0.001 × 6000 / 2 = 3 m

So a 1 ms timing precision at 6 km/s is a 3 m depth resolution.

Exam angle. Convert units first (km/s to m/s). Remember TWT is down and back, so halve it. For "why seismic over gravity and magnetic": seismic gives the shape and depth of structures in detail, and is the only one used for detailed surveys and well placement.
notes.4:
Reserves are an oil company's main assets. Estimating them is hard (the data can be interpreted in very different ways, and the development plan and operating practice change the answer) and it is an ongoing job through exploration, development planning and production. A reserve estimate is "little more than an educated guess", but an important one, because it drives company policy.

Learning outcomes. Be able to: explain reserves and the deterministic and probabilistic methods · discuss the uncertainty and how it changes during field life · draw and read the probability vs recoverable reserves curve showing proved, proved + probable and proved + probable + possible · use the volumetric equation for oil in place · calculate reserve estimates.

Reserve definitions

Reserves are the quantities of petroleum anticipated to be commercially recovered from known accumulations from a given date forward.
  • All estimates carry uncertainty, depending mainly on the amount of reliable geological and engineering data available at the time and how it is interpreted.
  • The 1987 Society of Petroleum Engineers / World Petroleum Congress definitions are accepted world-wide.
  • Proved reserves are the most certain. Unproved reserves are less certain and are split into probable and possible, with progressively greater uncertainty. Take care when adding up reserves of different classes.

Deterministic vs probabilistic

DeterministicProbabilistic
ApproachA single best estimate from known geological, engineering and economic dataUses the same data to generate a range of estimates with probabilities (e.g. Monte Carlo methods)
ResultOne numberA probability curve

Both involve some subjectivity.

Volume in-place calculations

Before any production, a volumetric estimate is made. Geological and geophysical data give contour maps, from which the hydrocarbon-bearing rock volume is estimated (with a planimeter and other tools). Well-log petrophysics gives average porosity and water saturation. Applying a recovery factor and the formation volume factor gives recoverable oil. Material balance is another method.

Recoverable oil = Vb × φ × (1 - Sw) × RF / Bo
SymbolMeaningUnits
VbBulk reservoir volumereservoir bbl
φPorosityfraction
(1 - Sw)Hydrocarbon saturation (assuming only water and hydrocarbon, so saturations sum to 1)fraction
RFRecovery factorfraction
BoOil formation volume factorres bbl / STB

Without the RF the same expression gives STOIIP (stock-tank oil initially in place). Dividing by Bo converts reservoir barrels to stock-tank barrels at surface conditions.

How the recovery factor is chosen

  • Lab measurement of oil displacement in cores (the residual oil saturation).
  • The type of displacement mechanism involved.
  • A correlation of sweep efficiency from a similar reservoir.

Worked example

Bulk volume 500 MM res bbl, φ = 0.20, Sw = 0.25, Bo = 1.2 res bbl/STB, RF = 0.35.

STOIIP = 500 × 0.20 × (1 - 0.25) / 1.2 = 62.5 MMSTB Recoverable = 62.5 × 0.35 = 21.9 MMSTB

Probabilistic representation

Each input in the equation is given a probability function (low, medium, high). Combining them gives a cumulative probability curve of the probability that reserves are greater than or equal to a chosen volume.

CategoryWhere on the curveMeaning
ProvedThe volume at P90 (90% probability)90% chance of at least this much
ProbableThe difference between P50 and P90Adding it to proved gives the P50 case
PossibleThe difference between P10 and P50Adding it to proved + probable gives the P10 case

Example from the notes: proved = 500 MMstb (P90); probable = 240 MMstb, so proved + probable = 740 MMstb (P50); possible = 120 MMstb, so proved + probable + possible = 860 MMstb (P10).

P90 = 500 P50 = 500 + 240 = 740 P10 = 740 + 120 = 860 (MMstb)
Common slip. P90 is the low number. It is the volume you are 90% sure of exceeding. Probable and possible are increments, not totals, unless the question asks for the cumulative P50 or P10 value.

Reserve estimates during reservoir life

As production continues and better information arrives, uncertainty reduces: the probability curve narrows as probability figures are gradually converted into recovery. Estimates are revised as new geological or engineering data arrive or as economics change. Even so, an estimate is needed early, and it is important to ask how far the project's viability depends on reserves being much greater or smaller than the "central estimate". This sensitivity can be tackled probabilistically by estimating the spread for one parameter about its mean (e.g. by Monte Carlo simulation, which is beyond this course).

StageHow reserves are estimated
Geophysical explorationOrder-of-magnitude estimate to rank projects before bidding. Volume of the structure from seismic maps, plus local geological trends that suggest the thickness of porous beds. Apply common ranges: porosity 7 to 30%, water saturation 8 to 40%, recovery factor 10 to 50%.
Exploration (discovery well)The uncertainty about whether hydrocarbons exist is removed, and measured porosity and water saturation exist for the section drilled. If logs corroborate the seismic, only the contour of the hydrocarbon-water contact (OWC) is needed for a reasonable estimate.
Field developmentMore wells define the volume, geometry and average porosity and saturation more accurately. Injection and withdrawal change the fluid interfaces, so the inventory is continuously updated (by computer or by hand, same principles).
notes.5:
Pressure and temperature underground control how fluids behave and how a reservoir is drilled and produced. This chapter separates the pressure from the rock weight above (lithostatic) from the pressure of the fluid in the pores, shows how to calculate pressure in the water, oil and gas zones, and covers geothermal temperature.

Learning outcomes. Be able to: define lithostatic, hydrostatic and pore pressure · distinguish normal, over- and under-pressured reservoirs · state the equations (with a sketch) · discuss causes of abnormal pressure · explain normal reservoir temperature · calculate reservoir temperature and pressure in the water, oil and gas zones.

Lithostatic and pore pressure

At depth two kinds of pressure exist:

  • Lithostatic (geostatic / overburden) pressure: caused by the weight of the rock, transmitted through grain-to-grain contacts. Gradient about 1 psi/ft. With that gradient, Pob = 1.0 × D psig at depth D in ft. The gradient varies with depth, overburden density, and how far the rock is supported by water pressure.
  • Fluid (pore) pressure: pressure of the fluid in the pore space. It balances part of the geostatic load, with the rest carried by the compacted grains.
  • In unconsolidated, loose sands the fluid supports all the overburden, so Pf = Pob.
  • In deposited formations like reservoir rock the fluid is not supporting the rock above. Its pressure comes from the continuity of the water phase from the surface down to depth D: the hydrostatic pressure, imposed by a column of fluid at rest. It depends on water density, which depends on salinity: Pf = ρw g D.

Fluid pressure in a hydrocarbon accumulation is set by the water pressure around the reservoir. In a normal situation:

pw = (dp/dD)w × D + 14.7 (psia, D in ft)

This assumes water pressure is continuous from the surface and salinity is constant. In practice water sands separated by impermeable shale still give hydrostatic continuity if any seal is broken, but salinity can vary with depth. A reservoir whose water pressure gradient, extrapolated to zero depth, gives atmospheric pressure (14.7 psi) is a normally pressured reservoir.

Hydrostatic pressure

Hydrostatic pressure is the pressure exerted by fluid at rest at a point, from the fluid density and the vertical height of the column:

P = ρ g h (ρg is a force per volume term: N/m³, so P is in Pa)

In field units ρg is usually given as density in lb/gal. To get psi/ft use 1 lb/gal = 0.0519 psi/ft (from 1 ft³ = 7.48 gal and 1 ft² = 144 in²). Example: fresh water at 8.34 lb/gal gives 8.34 × 0.0519 = 0.433 psi/ft. Salinity raises it: about 0.45 psi/ft for 55,000 ppm saline water.

FluidDensity, g/cm³Density, lb/galGradient, psi/ft
Fresh water1.008.340.433
Salt water1.159.590.498
Oil0.806.670.346
Gas0.181.540.080

So in a vertical column of fresh water, pressure is 0.433 psi greater for every extra foot of depth.

Overburden stress

Overburden pressure at a point is the pressure from the total weight of everything above it:

S = ∫ ρ(z) dz S(psi) = 0.433 ∫ ρ(z) dz (ρ in g/cm³, z in ft) conversion: 1 g/cm³ = 0.433 psi/ft

Bulk density depends on the rock matrix, the fluid and the porosity:

ρb = φ ρf + (1 - φ) ρm
  • As porosity → 0, ρb → ρm (the matrix). As porosity → 1, ρb → ρf (the fluid).
  • A thick sequence has bulk density about 2.3 g/cc ≈ 1 psi/ft (2.3 × 0.433).
  • Onshore the overburden gradient is close to 1 psi/ft. Offshore it can be lower, about 0.7 psi/ft, because of sea depth and the air gap.
LithologyGrain density, g/cm³
Sandstone2.65
Limestone2.71
Dolomite2.87
Anhydrite2.98
Halite2.03
Gypsum2.35
Clay2.70 to 2.80

Abnormal pressure

  • Normal: water pressure is hydrostatic from the surface (gradient about 0.433 to 0.45 psi/ft).
  • Overpressured: pore pressure is above normal.
  • Underpressured: pore pressure is below normal.
pw = (dp/dD)w × D + 14.7 + C C > 0 overpressured C < 0 underpressured

The gradient is the same as normal; the line is shifted sideways by the constant C. In abnormally pressured reservoirs the sand is sealed off from the surrounding strata, so there is no hydrostatic continuity to the surface. On the sketch the lithostatic line (about 1 psi/ft) is the overburden pressure that pore pressure normally stays below.

Causes of abnormal pore pressure

  • Thermal effects: water that cannot escape expands or contracts with temperature. A 1 °F rise can add about 125 psi in a sealed fresh-water system.
  • Clay diagenesis: montmorillonite turning into illite releases water as the clay compacts. If it cannot escape, fluid pressure rises.
  • Osmosis: clay acts as a semipermeable membrane, so water crosses it if there are different salt solutions either side. Related: electro-osmosis (chemical reactions create an electric potential and water movement) and thermo-osmosis (a temperature difference across the barrier).
  • Tectonism: folding or faulting moves sediment to a depth different from where it was deposited, so its pressure no longer matches its new depth.
  • Rapid burial of sand and clay layers: fluids cannot escape from the pores fast enough.
  • Depletion: production from the reservoir, natural or man-made, lowers pressure.

Pore pressure calculation: water, oil and gas zones

Take a normally pressured sequence. Depths measured from surface: x = depth to the oil-water contact (OWC), y = depth to the gas-oil contact (GOC), h = depth of interest.

Assumptions: all pores are filled with water originally; pores are interconnected; transition zones between fluids are small; density barely changes with depth. Then dp = ρ g dh, and between two depths p2 - p1 = ρ g (h2 - h1).

Water: pw(h) - psurface = ρw g h Oil: po(h) - po(x) = ρo g (h - x) Gas: pg(h) - pg(y) = ρg g (h - y)

Pressure is continuous at the contacts (pw(x) = po(x) and po(y) = pg(y)), so building up from the water leg:

po(h) = psurface + ρw g x + ρo g (h - x) = psurface + (ρw - ρo) g x + ρo g h → po(h) = ρo g h + constant pg(h) = psurface + ρw g x + ρo g (y - x) + ρg g (h - y) = psurface + (ρw - ρo) g x + (ρo - ρg) g y + ρg g h → pg(h) = ρg g h + constant Gas straight on water (GWC at depth z): pg(h) = psurface + (ρw - ρg) g z + ρg g h

What it means: in each fluid the pressure line has that fluid's own gradient (steepest in water, shallower in oil, shallowest in gas), and the lines meet at the contacts. The oil and gas columns therefore sit at a higher pressure than the water at the same depth above the contact.

Worked example (illustrative numbers)

Normally pressured water gradient 0.45 psi/ft, oil 0.35 psi/ft, gas 0.08 psi/ft. OWC at 8000 ft, GOC at 7600 ft. Find the pressure at the OWC, at the GOC and at 7500 ft in the gas.

OWC (8000 ft): p = 0.45 × 8000 + 14.7 = 3614.7 psi GOC (7600 ft): p = 3614.7 - 0.35 × (8000 - 7600) = 3474.7 psi 7500 ft (gas): p = 3474.7 - 0.08 × (7600 - 7500) = 3466.7 psi

You go up from a contact by subtracting gradient × distance, using the gradient of the fluid in that zone.

Pore pressure measurement

Indirect methods (qualitative, indications only)

  • Surface pressures during a kick (flow of reservoir fluid into the well while drilling). Nobody drills for a kick just to measure pressure.
  • Log-derived fluid densities.
  • Seismic velocity analysis, which indicates formation compaction.
  • The mud density / gas relationship: differential pressure affects how much formation gas enters the mud.
  • The nature of the cuttings (fragmentation).
  • Drilling exponents: drillability is affected by the differential pressure at the bottom of the hole.
  • Shale density trends through the section being drilled.

Direct measurement (quantitative)

  • The first vertical pressure tools (mid-1950s) took one fluid sample and measured one formation pressure.
  • The Repeat Formation Tester (RFT), introduced in 1975, takes two fluid samples and unlimited pressure measurements. A probe is pushed through the mud cake to take small fluid volumes and pressures, so it only works in open hole, and it can be set at different depths.
  • The main application is a pressure-depth profile over the reservoir interval. From it you get fluid gradients, fluid contacts and reservoir characterisation, which supports better reservoir management and optimum production.

Reservoir temperature

Temperature rises from the Earth's surface towards the centre. Heat flow outward through the crust creates the geothermal gradient, which has local and regional variation from the thermal properties of the rock and from crustal thickness (ridges, rifts, plate boundaries).

  • In most petroleum basins the gradient is about 1.6 °F per 100 ft (0.029 K/m).
  • The reservoir and overburden have a large thermal capacity, and the porous reservoir has a large surface area, so flow processes in the reservoir can be assumed to happen at constant temperature.
  • Local gradient is affected by features such as volcanic intrusions and is found from wellbore temperature surveys, which must be taken under stabilised conditions (circulating or injected fluids cause transient cooling, which can be corrected by proper analysis).

Without a temperature survey, estimate temperature at vertical depth D from a typical gradient and a surface temperature of 15 °C (60 °F):

T(D) = 288.2 + (T.G.) × D (K, gradient in K/m, D in m) Field units: T(°F) = 60 + 1.6 × (D / 100)

Example: at 10,000 ft, T = 60 + 1.6 × 100 = 220 °F.

Exam angle. State the gradient you use and add 14.7 psi for atmospheric pressure when working in absolute pressure. For pressure in oil or gas zones, start at the contact and work up using that fluid's gradient.
